notes.question: This is the question a team bot gets every day: how many weeks of parental leave do we get?
notes.guess: The model answers twelve weeks, fluently and with confidence. Fluent is not the same as right.
notes.stamp: It cites nothing, because it never saw our handbook.
notes.handbook: The fact is in the handbook: section 4.2, sixteen weeks, paid. The model cannot see it. RAG has to bring it.

notes.index: Offline, once: the handbook is cut into chunks, each chunk becomes a vector, and the vectors are stored in an index. It is rebuilt only when the handbook changes.
notes.query: Online, for every question. The question is turned into a vector by the same model.
notes.search: The question's vector is compared with the stored vectors, and the closest ones win. The two lanes meet here.
notes.prompt: The best passages are copied into a prompt, together with the question and an instruction.
notes.llm: The LLM reads the prompt and writes the answer. It does not search your files: it only sees what is in the prompt.
notes.answer: The answer comes back with its section, so a person can check it against the handbook.

notes.page: One long document. Nobody can fit sixty pages in a prompt, and one vector for sixty pages would blur every topic.
notes.cut: So we cut it into chunks. Where the cut falls decides what can be found.
notes.overlap: Neighbouring chunks share a little text, so a sentence split by a cut still appears whole in one of them.
notes.chunk: This is what the search sees: a piece of text with its source. Too big and the answer gets lost; too small and the context is gone.

notes.chunks: Every chunk becomes a vector: a list of numbers. The plane shows only two, so it fits on a slide. Real vectors have hundreds.
notes.clusters: Chunks on the same topic end up close together. Closeness is meaning, not shared words.
notes.question: The question goes through the same step, and it lands next to section 4.2.
notes.numbers: Section 4.2 is [3, 4] and the question is [4, 3]. Next: how to measure how close two of them point.

notes.angle: The score is the cosine of the angle between two arrows. The question and section 4.2 differ by about 16 degrees: cosine 0.96.
notes.length: Length does not count. This longer copy of 4.2 points the same way, so it gets the same score.
notes.scale: The score runs from +1, same direction, to −1, opposite. Unrelated text sits near 0. Parking is at a right angle: 0.00.

notes.dot: The dot product multiplies matching numbers and adds them: 4 times 3, plus 3 times 4, is 24.
notes.lengths: Each length is Pythagoras on the vector's numbers: 5 and 5. Dividing by them removes the length of the text.
notes.score: 24 divided by 25 is 0.96. Almost the same direction: that is the score of section 4.2.
notes.zero: Parking: 4 times 3, plus 3 times minus 4, is zero. A right angle gives 0, whatever the lengths.

notes.compare: The question is compared with every chunk: one cosine each. The handbook is not read again.
notes.score: Each chunk gets a score. Section 4.2 is closest with 0.96; parking is at 0.00.
notes.top-k: Retrieval keeps the top k. Here k is 3, and it is a setting you choose. Large indexes use an approximate search instead of comparing every chunk.
notes.text: What comes back is text and its section number, not vectors. That text is what the model will read.

notes.instructions: The prompt is plain text. The instruction is part of the design: it tells the model to answer only from the passages and to cite them.
notes.passages: The passages come from the search, with their sections. The model sees only these.
notes.llm: The question joins the prompt, and the whole sheet goes to the LLM. The LLM does not search: it reads what you gave it.
notes.answer: It writes the answer one word at a time, each word predicted from the prompt. The source lets you check it against the passage.

elements.text: “How many weeks of parental leave do we get?”

notes.search: The vector is compared with every chunk. The best scores are 0.96, 0.94 and 0.92; parking gets 0.00.
notes.prompt: The top three chunks go into the prompt, with the instruction and the question.
notes.llm: The LLM reads the prompt and writes the answer.
notes.answer: Sixteen weeks, from section 4.2. Five steps from question to answer, and each one can be checked.

notes.split: A cut through a table can hide the answer: the 16-week row is split across two chunks.
notes.codes: A code such as HR-17 matches poorly by meaning. Exact terms may need keyword search as well.
notes.k: With k = 3, the passage with the answer ranks fourth and is dropped. A larger k adds context, and noise.
notes.guess: If no passage has the answer, the model may still answer. Allow it to say the answer is not in the handbook.

notes.set: A small set of questions with known sources is enough to start. Each one has its expected section.
notes.retrieval: Eight of ten have the right section in the top 3. If the section is not retrieved, no model can save the answer.
notes.answer: Of those eight, seven answers are supported by their passage. A fluent wrong answer looks like a right one.
notes.fix: Each failure points at one stage: chunks or k for retrieval, the prompt for answers. Change one, then run the set again.

notes.facts: Use RAG for facts that change, or that need a source. Re-indexing updates the answers without retraining the model.
notes.style: Style, format and behaviour need fine-tuning. RAG does not change how the model writes.
notes.small: If the text fits in the prompt, paste it. No index needed.
notes.idea: Close on the one idea: RAG finds the passages closest to the question, by cosine, and hands them to the model.
